text.p: So, how's your stomach? If the up-down-down, up-down-down Wall Street Waltz has you worried, you aren't alone. Never have so many had so much of their retirement funds tied up in a stock market they don't quite understand.

Mix in a dose of here-comes-the-bear pronouncements, a concerted effort by the Federal Reserve Board chairman to break the market's momentum, and a bull market in ever-conflicting financial advice, and it's no wonder everyone's feeling nervous and confused about what to do.
You can expect the market to be volatile for a while. Nobody knows whether this is a transition to a better market or a worse one, but a transition it is.

With see-sawing the order of the day, you'll need to protect yourself a bit without jerking your portfolio around every time the market jerks. Get back in touch with your own investment philosophy and these investing basics and then don't worry, be happy.

-- The best way to win with long term investments remains the same: Invest steadily in a mix of investments that balance each other. If you've left your portfolio on autopilot for a couple of years, you may have way more in the stock market, and especially those blue-chip winners, than you originally intended.

Decide your best investment mix, such as 70 percent stocks, 20 percent bonds and 10 percent liquid savings, and stick with it. That means that you might have to move some money out of your winners every year over to your losers. Besides keeping you in balance, that forces you to buy low and sell high.

-- Diversify among stocks, too. If all of your stock market money is in a Standard & Poor's 500 index fund, shift some into foreign stocks, small company stocks, mid company stocks and bargain-priced so-called "value" stocks.

-- Don't bail altogether. This market hasn't even begun to test your long term resolve, but it may. If it does, remember that the biggest investment losers are not those people who stay in through thick and thin. It's the people who pull out when times are bad and fail to get back in on time for the good times.

A University of Michigan study proved this: Investors who were in the market for 1,276 trading days received 26.3 percent a year on their money. If they missed the 40 biggest days, their return would only have been 4.3 percent a year. And those biggest days typically come on the heels of bad days. Famed investor Bernard Baruch observed that only liars manage to always be out during bad times and in during good times.

-- Don't fall for the bond market trap. It's true that over very long periods of time, bonds balance stocks, but it's not as true as you might think. There are many periods when bonds and stocks move in tandem.

During periods of rising interest rates, both bonds and stocks are apt to do badly at the same time. Long-term investors can diversify their stocks with short-term bonds, money market funds, inflation-fighting investments, and just a smattering of long-term bonds, unless they need the quick income a long-term bond can provide.

-- Keep a piece of your portfolio set aside to fight inflation. You can do this buy buying the Treasury's new inflation-proof bonds, or by buying shares in a mutual fund that focuses on real estate, gold, or other commodities, or by having a real estate investment on the side. Inflation remains comparatively low, and may stay that way for years. Think of this piece of your portfolio as insurance: Maybe you'll never need it, but you'll be glad to have it if you do.
-- Pay attention to price. If you liked a stock when it was $60 a share, why not like it more at $55 or $50? When markets fall, look for bargains in solid companies with good earnings records.

-- Keep your expenses down. Maybe when your stocks are returning 30 percent a year, you don't care about the mutual fund that skims off 2 percent or 3 percent. But if you live through a flat or down market, those expenses are going to hurt.

One way to keep yourself from trading too rapidly during volatile markets is to take your time doing research instead of buying and selling. Spend your nervous energy finding the lowest cost funds that accomplish what you'd like for the different sectors in which you invest. Then take your time to move your money, rebalancing as you do.
